Subject: .Salmonella/Microsome (S/M) Assay -- Effects of Reverse Phase
Chromatography of Burley CEL Soluble Fraction (BuS1)
Reverse phase liquid chromatography methodology was used by M. Core and
R. Izac to separate a burley CEL soluble fraction (BuSl) into two fractions
(F1 and F2). A complete description of the fractionation scheme and the
resulting samples has been documented (l). No sharp distinctions between
the two fractions were observed based upon chromatographic analysis (1).
The weight ratio of fraction 1 to fraction 2 was found to be about 3:1 (1).
These samples, along with a BuSl control were oversprayed onto bright
baseweb (Br Bw) and made into cigarettes (2). The IT CSCs from these test
and control cigarettes were evaluated in the S/M assay to determine any
differential activities (3).
The four smokings from each sample as well as the preparation of the
CSCs (10 mg/ml) were done by members of Project 6912 (2,4) and stored at
-80°C until tested. The CSC yield data are shown in Table 1. It should be
noted that the F2 cigarette had a substantially higher CSC yield than both
the control and Fl cigarette (-70% higher). F2 was visibly much darker in
color than Fl (5). All samples were tested randomly according to the
standard test procedures (3,6). As shown in the addendum, the control data
were within the normal ranges. The attached experimental data demonstrate
that dose-responses were observed for these samples and that the responses
were at least twice the background level.
Table 1 also gives the results from the four smokings and analysis of
variance (performed using "Minitab"). There were no differences among the
control (BuSl cigarettes) and the cigarettes made with the two test
fractions. However, a closer look at the data suggests that the higher
slope value for smoking 3 of the F2 cigarette is an obvious outlier
influencing the separation of means. When the slope value for smoking 3 of
the F2 cigarette was omitted from the analysis, F2 CSC was significantly
lower in specific activity (S.A.) than F1 CSC and the CSC control. While
this finding may indicate that the chromatography utilized did produce a
less active fraction, there is no evidence from the S/M assay that would
invalidate any of the data obtained and reported here (including the outlier
from smoking 3 of the F2 cigarette). Therefore, the initial conclusions
drawn from Table 1 (no differences among any samples) will remain.
Additionally, the magnitude of differences in S.A.s among the samples is not
enough to warrant a retest for further validation of these results. Because
the crossed soluble/baseweb study is ongoing, other fractionation schemes
will be applied in an effort to identify active components.
